title: How LLM APIs work
summary: What really happens when Notely's Summarize button calls the Claude API: tokens, messages, the context window, output limits and picking a model.
youWillLearn: What a token is, and why it is the unit of cost, speed and limits
Why the API has no memory, and what the messages list is for
What the context window and max_tokens limit, and how to spot a cut-off answer
How to choose a model per feature, and where the API key must live

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.LLM: Large language model: a program trained on huge amounts of text that continues a piece of text by predicting what comes next.
glossary.token: A small chunk of text, often a short word or part of a word. Models read, write and bill in tokens.
glossary.system prompt: Standing instructions sent with every request, separate from the conversation, that set the model's role and rules.
glossary.messages: The list of turns in a conversation, each marked as from the user or the assistant, sent in full with every request.
glossary.context window: The maximum number of tokens a model can take in one request: instructions, conversation, documents and its own answer together.
glossary.max_tokens: A request setting that caps how many tokens the model may write in its answer. When it is hit, the answer stops mid-sentence.
glossary.stop_reason: A field in the API response that says why the model stopped: it finished, it hit max_tokens, it wants to use a tool, and so on.
glossary.temperature: A setting on many LLM APIs that controls how random the word choices are. Low is more predictable, high is more varied.
glossary.env var: Environment variable: a named setting kept outside the code, like a model id or a secret key, that the server reads when it runs.
glossary.API key: A secret string that proves a request comes from your account. Anyone holding it can spend your money.

steps.title: Notely's Summarize button
body: Notely is our course's notes app. Maya, one of its users, opens a long note in her browser (the screen she types into) and clicks Summarize.
The browser sends the click to the app server (the computer running Notely's code). The app server sends the note's text to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI. Three short lines come back.

scene.caption: Maya's click travels through the app server to the Claude API and back.

steps.title: The last step is a black box
body: You built this with Claude Code, and it works. But a client asks: why does it cost what it costs? Why do very long notes fail? Why did one summary stop mid-sentence?
You cannot answer yet, because the answers all live inside that one call from the app server to the Claude API. This lesson opens it up.
changes: ~ Maya and Browser step back
~ Claude API in focus: what happens inside it?

scene.caption: Everything this lesson explains happens on the last arrow.

steps.title: A model guesses the next piece of text
body: Behind the Claude API is an LLM. Given some text, it predicts the next small piece, adds it, and predicts again, until it decides to stop.
Those pieces are tokens, often a short word or part of a longer one. Your note goes in as tokens. The summary comes back as tokens, one at a time.

callout.text: The model samples its next token, so the same note can get different wording twice. Many APIs have a temperature knob for this; newer Claude models reject it. Never build a feature that needs identical words every time.

changes: ~ Claude API: writes the answer one token at a time

scene.caption: The answer comes back one token after another.

steps.title: Tokens are the unit of everything
body: Providers bill per token, with separate prices for input (what you send) and output (what the model writes). Output tokens usually cost several times more.
Tokens also set speed, because the model writes one at a time, and limits, because every model has a ceiling. So Maya's 40-page note costs more and takes longer than a shopping list.

callout.text: Every API response includes a usage object with input and output token counts. Log it from day one. It is the only honest answer to "what does this feature cost?"

changes: ~ Tokens in 800 → 30,000: a 40-page note
~ Claude API pill: next token → 30,000 in

scene.caption: A bigger note means more tokens in: more cost, more time.

steps.title: The API has no memory
body: Each call starts from zero. The model does not remember Maya's last request. So the app server sends everything, every time: a system prompt with standing rules, plus a list of messages.
In a chat, that list holds the whole conversation so far and grows each turn. That is why long chats get slower and more expensive.

code.caption: One request: standing rules, the conversation, and a cap on the answer's length.

changes: + Messages: the rules and full conversation, sent every call
~ Claude API pill removed

scene.caption: The app server packs the whole conversation into every request.

steps.title: The context window is a desk, not a shelf
body: The context window is the most the model can look at in one request: system prompt, messages, documents and its own answer, all counted in tokens.
It is a hard limit. Maya uploads a 300-page PDF, and the API rejects the request. Even below the limit, stuffing in everything "just in case" costs more and can make answers worse.

callout.text: A desk holds only what fits on it right now. Your database is the shelf. Lesson 5 is about fetching the right pages from the shelf instead of dumping all of them on the desk.

changes: ~ Messages: now holds a 300-page PDF
~ Tokens in 30,000 → 400,000: over the window
~ Claude API rejects the request

scene.caption: Too many tokens: the request never reaches the model.

steps.title: Answers have a length cap
body: You also set max_tokens: the most the model may write. Say someone lowers it to 50 to save money. Maya's summary needs 60, so it stops mid-sentence, with no error.
Each response says why it ended in stop_reason: end_turn means finished, max_tokens means cut off. Check it before saving, or Notely stores half a bullet.

code.caption: A cut-off answer still arrives as a normal success. Only stop_reason tells you.

changes: ~ Tokens in 400,000 → 2,000: a normal note again
~ Tokens out 60 → 50: the answer hit the cap
~ Stop reason end_turn → max_tokens
~ Messages back to normal; Claude API answers, cut short

scene.caption: The answer arrives without an error, but it was cut off.

steps.title: Pick a model per feature
body: Models come in sizes, all behind the Claude API. Small ones are fast and cheap; large ones reason better but cost more and take longer.
Notely's summary runs fine on a small model; "plan my week from 200 notes" may need a large one. Keep each model id in an env var (a setting outside the code).

callout.text: Ask: which model does each feature use, and why? Is the model id in an env var or hard-coded in five files? Is max_tokens set and stop_reason checked? Model names change often: ask it to check the current list.

changes: − Claude API and Messages: we look at the models behind the API
+ Small Model: fast and cheap, for summaries
+ Large Model: slower, for hard planning
~ Cap back to 1,024: Tokens out 50 → 60, Stop reason → end_turn

scene.caption: The app server sends each feature to the model that fits it.

steps.title: The API key stays on the server
body: The API key pays for every token. If it reaches the browser, anyone can copy it and run their own app on your bill.

The classic slip: an env var named NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. That prefix tells Next.js, the toolkit Notely is built with, to ship the value to every visitor. Only the app server should hold the key.

callout.text: Bots find leaked keys within hours of a public push. If one leaks, rotate it in the provider console right away, then check the usage page.

changes: − Small Model and Large Model
+ Claude API: back, holding the bill
+ Someone Else: a stranger calling Claude with the copied key
~ Browser now carries the key: a mistake

scene.caption: A key in the browser lets a stranger call Claude on Notely's bill.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: An LLM predicts the next token, over and over: tokens are what you pay for, wait for and run out of. The API remembers nothing, so every call carries the rules and all messages, and it must fit in the context window.
Cap answers with max_tokens, check stop_reason, use the smallest model that works, keep the key on the server.
changes: − Someone Else: the key lives only on the app server
~ Browser safe again; every part working

scene.caption: One click, one call, the key safely on the server.

quiz.question: Notely's chat feature gets slower and more expensive the longer Maya chats. Why?

options.text: The model gets tired after many messages.
options.why: Models have no state between calls. Nothing about the model changes during a chat.

options.text: Each request re-sends the whole conversation, so input tokens grow every turn.
options.why: The API has no memory. The messages list carries the full history, so every turn adds tokens to every later call.

options.text: The provider charges a fee per message, rising over time.
options.why: Billing is per token, not per message. The cost grows because the token count grows.

quiz.question: Some saved summaries end mid-sentence, but the logs show only successful responses. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The database column is too short.
options.why: Possible in theory, but the classic cause is the model's cap. Check the response before blaming storage.

options.text: The answer hit max_tokens; stop_reason would say so.
options.why: Hitting the output cap is not an error. The response looks like a normal success, and only stop_reason: "max_tokens" reveals the cut.

options.text: The network dropped the end of the response.
options.why: A dropped connection usually shows up as an error, not as a clean success with a shorter answer.

quiz.question: Claude Code put NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env so a page can call the Claude API directly. What do you ask for?

options.text: Keep it, but minify the JavaScript so the key is hard to find.
options.why: Minifying does not hide strings. Anyone can open dev tools and find the key in seconds.

options.text: Keep it, since the repository is private.
options.why: The repo being private does not matter. The key ships to every visitor's browser when the page loads.

options.text: Rename it without the prefix and move the call into a server route the page calls.
options.why: The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix bundles the value into browser code. A server-only env var plus your own route keeps the key secret.

takeaways: An LLM writes one token at a time. Tokens are the unit of cost, speed and limits.
The API has no memory: every call sends the system prompt and the full messages list.
Everything, including the answer, must fit in the context window. More context is not always better.
Set max_tokens and check stop_reason: a cut-off answer still arrives as a success.
Pick the smallest model that does each job well, keep its id in an env var, and keep the API key on the server.
